Taxed on inflation: how much of a long-held fund’s capital gain is just higher prices

Canada taxes the capital gain in dollars, not in purchasing power, so the part of a gain that merely keeps up with inflation is taxed like real profit. See how big that part is for a fund held for decades, how it raises the true tax rate on your real return, what September CPI since 2006 implies, and why a TFSA or RRSP changes the arithmetic.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

How much of your capital gain is only inflation, and what the tax on it does to your real return

$10,000 grows 4% a year in real terms while prices rise 2.5% a year, a nominal return of 6.60%. In a taxable account the units are sold in year 20; half of the nominal gain is taxed at 29.65%, so the statutory rate on a gain is 14.825%. Canada does not index the cost base for inflation, so the part of the gain that only restores purchasing power is taxed too. The interest comparison taxes the same nominal return in full every year, which is how GIC or bond-fund interest is taxed. The model ignores yearly fund distributions, fees and changes in tax law; returns are hypothetical, not a forecast. A capital loss is valued as if it could be used at the same rate.

The central idea

A capital gain on a fund includes a portion that only restores purchasing power, and in a taxable account that portion is taxed too, because the cost base is not adjusted for inflation. With 4% real growth and 2.5% inflation over 20 years, about a quarter of the reported gain is inflation, and tax takes 19.7% of the real gain instead of the 14.8% headline rate. Interest taxed every year fares far worse. Inside a TFSA neither part is taxed.

01

A gain on paper, a gain in tax, and a smaller gain in life

Suppose you bought a balanced or equity fund in a non-registered account 20 years ago, and its units are now worth more than three and a half times what you paid. The tax return calls the difference a capital gain. But groceries, rent and wages also rose over those 20 years. Part of the “gain” is just the same purchasing power expressed in more dollars.

Canada taxes the dollar gain: the proceeds minus the adjusted cost base, as CRA’s capital gains guide defines it, with no allowance for inflation. Half of that gain is included in income. This guide asks how much of the gain is inflation, how much tax falls on it, and what that does to the tax rate on the part of the return that actually made you better off.

The answer is not a reason to avoid investing or to fear inflation. It is a reason to understand why the account you hold a fund in matters, and why a low-return investment held in a taxable account can lose purchasing power even when it shows a profit.

02

Chart 1: splitting the reported gain

With the defaults, $10,000 grows 4% a year in real terms while prices rise 2.5% a year, a nominal return of 6.6%. After 20 years the units are worth about $35,904 and the reported gain is about $25,904.

To buy what $10,000 bought at the start, you would need about $16,386 at the end. So $6,386, about a quarter of the reported gain, is inflation. The other $19,518 is the real gain, measured in the dollars of the sale year.

At a 29.65% marginal rate and half inclusion, the tax on the sale is about $3,840. About $947 of it falls on the inflation part, which bought you nothing. The waterfall shows the four pieces: real gain, inflation, tax on each.

03

The tax rate on what you really gained

Measure everything in today’s purchasing power. Without tax, the fund would have turned $10,000 into $21,911 of today’s money, a real gain of $11,911. After the tax at sale it is worth $19,568, a real gain of $9,568. Tax took 19.7% of the real gain, not the 14.8% (half of 29.65%) that the headline rate suggests.

The heatmap repeats this for real growth from 1% to 6% and inflation from 0% to 6% over the holding period you enter. With no inflation every cell equals the headline rate. With high inflation and low real growth the effective rate climbs: at 1% real growth and 4% inflation over 20 years, tax takes about half of the real gain. That combination, a cautious investment in a high-inflation period, is exactly when the tax on inflation hurts most.

Longer holding helps a little: the deferral of tax until sale lets the untaxed amount compound, and the real part of the gain grows faster than the inflation part when real returns are healthy.

04

Chart 3: what the CPI since 2006 implies

The third chart uses Statistics Canada’s all-items CPI (table 18-10-0004-01) for September of each year from 2006 to 2025 and for September 2026 (170.0). It shows how much $10,000 invested in each September had to grow by September 2026 just to keep its purchasing power, and the tax that rise alone would bring if sold in a taxable account at the entered rate.

From September 2006 (CPI 109.2) the required rise is about $5,568, so the units had to be worth $15,568 just to break even in real terms; selling at that price would bring about $825 of tax at 29.65% on a real gain of zero. From September 2021 the required rise is about $1,896 because of the high inflation of 2021 to 2023. These are dated observations; the tax column is a calculation at your entered rate.

The same arithmetic means a fund that only kept pace with inflation, sold in a taxable account, leaves you with less purchasing power than you started with.

05

Chart 4: account and income type matter more than the fund

The last chart follows the same pre-tax return three ways, in today’s dollars. Inside a TFSA nothing is taxed, so the real value grows at the full 4%. In a taxable account with the gain taxed only at sale, the value trails the TFSA by the tax on both parts of the gain. If the same nominal return were paid as interest and taxed in full every year, as GIC interest and much of a bond fund’s distribution are, the real after-tax return falls to about 2.1% a year and tax takes about 57% of the real gain.

This is why the taxable interest guide finds that savings deposits can lose purchasing power after tax, and why balanced funds, which hold bonds, distribute more taxable income each year than equity funds. The income-type guide compares interest, dividends and gains.

Note the distinction. A TFSA or RRSP is an account with tax rules; it does not change the fund’s risk, fees or returns. An RRSP defers tax rather than removing it: withdrawals are fully taxed as income, so it removes the inflation-on-gains problem but taxes the whole withdrawal at your rate at that time.

06

What to do with this

  1. Use the tax-free and tax-deferred room for long-held growth first. The longer you expect to hold, and the higher inflation might be, the more the TFSA’s freedom from tax on both real and inflation gains is worth. The asset location guide discusses what to put where.
  2. Separate new pay from an existing holding. Contributing future savings to a TFSA is simple. Moving an existing non-registered fund into a TFSA is a sale for tax purposes, and the inflation part of its gain is taxed then; the in-kind contribution guide explains.
  3. Do not sell early to “reset” the gain. Realizing gains sooner only pays the tax sooner. Deferral is valuable; the gain timing guide shows it.
  4. Judge returns in real, after-tax terms. A fund that shows a 50% gain over 15 years may have made far less in purchasing power. Compare plans in today’s dollars, as the inflation and purchasing-power guide does.
  5. Keep perspective on risk. Equity and balanced funds can fall sharply and recover slowly; no return here is promised. Tax arithmetic matters, but diversification, fees and staying invested matter more.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The half inclusion of capital gains and the unindexed cost base follow CRA’s capital gains guidance reviewed 26 October 2026. September CPI values from 2006 to 2026 are dated observations from Statistics Canada. Real growth, inflation, holding period and tax rate are hypothetical editable inputs, not a forecast of any fund’s return. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 (page date 2026-02-05): a capital gain is the proceeds of disposition minus the adjusted cost base and outlays; the worked example taxes 50% of the gain. The page describes no inflation adjustment of the cost base.

    September values 2006–2026 (2002=100), retrieved through the Bank of Canada Valet API on 26 October 2026: 109.2 (2006), 142.9 (2021), 164.9 (2025), 170.0 (2026).

    Republishes the Statistics Canada series above; JSON retrieved 26 October 2026 (SHA-256 recorded in the local release note).

    Reviewed by earlier TickerLantern guides on 25–26 October 2026: federal 20.5% and Ontario 9.15% bracket rates give the 29.65% default combined rate. Your own rate depends on your province and income.
